summary: Describes an RTP payload format for comfort noise, the soft background hiss played during silence. It is for audio codecs, like G.711, that cannot carry comfort noise themselves.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3389 defines a small packet format for sending a description of background noise over RTP. It is meant for voice codecs that cannot make a background hiss themselves. The sender measures how loud the room is and, optionally, what the noise sounds like, and puts that in one short packet. The receiver then makes its own noise from the description, so a silent call still sounds like a real room rather than a dead line.

questions: how is comfort noise sent over rtp
what is a silence insertion descriptor
subtitle: A tiny RTP payload that tells the listener how loud and what color the background hiss should be during silence.

tldr.problem: When a voice codec has nothing to send because the speaker is silent, the receiver's line goes dead. Sending silence itself wastes bandwidth, but sending nothing means the listener hears no background noise at all and the call sounds broken.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a small RTP payload that describes the background noise instead of carrying speech. The first byte gives the noise level, and optional further bytes give reflection coefficients that describe the shape of the noise, so the receiver can generate a similar hiss locally.
tldr.outcome: The payload is registered as static RTP payload type 13, and it is meant for codecs such as G.711, G.726, G.727, G.728 and G.722 that cannot produce comfort noise themselves. The memo fixes only the format, leaving the voice activity detection, the choice of when to send a packet, and the noise synthesis to each implementation.

facts.label: Payload length
facts.value: M+1 bytes, where M is the model order

facts.label: MIME type
facts.value: audio/CN, with an optional rate parameter defaulting to 8000

today: RFC 3389 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It registers the static RTP payload type 13 for comfort noise and the audio/CN media type, and it is based on the comfort noise payload format defined in Appendix II of ITU-T Recommendation G.711.

sections.title: What Comfort Noise Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3389 describes an RTP payload format for transporting comfort noise. The CN payload type is primarily for use with audio codecs that do not support comfort noise as part of the codec itself, such as ITU-T Recommendations G.711, G.726, G.727, G.728 and G.722.

The payload format is based on Appendix II of ITU-T Recommendation G.711, which defines a comfort noise payload format, or bit-stream, for G.711 use in packet-based multimedia communication systems. It is generic, and may also be used with other audio codecs without built-in discontinuous transmission capability. It provides a minimum interoperability specification for the communication of comfort noise parameters, while the comfort noise analysis and synthesis, the voice activity detection and the discontinuous transmission algorithms are unspecified and left implementation-specific.

An example solution for G.711 has been tested and is described in the appendix. It uses the voice activity detection and discontinuous transmission of G.729 Annex B and a comfort noise generation algorithm that the appendix provides for information.

The comfort noise payload, also known as a Silence Insertion Descriptor frame, consists of a single octet description of the noise level and may contain spectral information in subsequent octets. An earlier version of the format, consisting only of the noise level byte, was defined in draft revisions of RFC 1890. The extended format defined here is backward compatible with implementations of that earlier version, on the assumption that only the first byte is interpreted and any additional spectral information bytes are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Some voice codecs cannot make background noise themselves, so a call goes completely silent when the speaker stops. This payload sends a short description of the room noise instead, and the receiver makes its own noise from it. The memo fixes the format of that description and leaves the rest to each implementation.

sections.title: The Noise Level Byte
sections.content:
The comfort noise payload consists of a description of the noise level and, optionally, spectral information in the form of reflection coefficients for an all-pole model of the noise. The inclusion of the spectral information is optional and the model order, that is the number of coefficients, is left unspecified. The encoder may choose a model order based on quality, complexity, expected environmental noise and signal bandwidth.

The model order is not explicitly transmitted, because the number of coefficients can be derived from the length of the payload at the receiver. The decoder may reduce the model order by setting the higher order reflection coefficients to zero, if it wants to reduce complexity or for other reasons.

The magnitude of the noise level is packed into the least significant bits of the noise level byte, with the most significant bit unused and always set to zero. The least significant bit of the noise level magnitude is packed into the least significant bit of the byte.

The noise level is expressed in dBov, with values from 0 to 127 representing 0 to -127 dBov. dBov is the level relative to the overload of the system. The memo notes that a representation relative to the overload point of a system is particularly useful for digital implementations, since one does not need to know the relative calibration of the analogue circuitry. For example, in a u-law system the reference would be a square wave with values of plus or minus 8031, and that square wave represents 0 dBov, which translates into 6.18 dBm0.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte says how loud the background noise is, in steps of one decibel below the point where the system would distort. The top bit of the byte is always zero, so the level uses the other seven bits and can run from 0 down to -127 dBov.

sections.title: Spectral Information and Payload Packing
sections.content:
The spectral information is transmitted using reflection coefficients. Each reflection coefficient can have values between -1 and 1 and is quantized uniformly using 8 bits. The quantized value is represented by the 8 bit index N, where N runs from 0 to 254, and index 255 is reserved for future use. Each index is packed into a separate byte, most significant bit first. The quantized value of a reflection coefficient k_i is obtained from its index by the formula in the memo.

The first byte of the payload must contain the noise level. The quantized reflection coefficients are packed in subsequent bytes in ascending order, where M is the model order, and the total length of the payload is M+1 bytes. A 0th order model, that is one with no spectral envelope information, reduces to transmitting only the energy level.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extra byte describes one stage of a model of the background noise, as a number between minus one and one. The byte holds an index rather than the number itself, so the receiver can turn the index back into a coefficient with a simple calculation. A payload with no extra bytes says only how loud the noise is.

sections.title: Using the Payload with RTP
sections.content:
The RTP header for a comfort noise packet should be constructed as if the comfort noise were an independent codec, so the RTP timestamp designates the beginning of the comfort noise period. When the payload format is used under the RTP profile of RFC 1890, a static payload type of 13 is assigned for an RTP timestamp clock rate of 8,000 Hz. If other rates are needed, they must be defined through dynamic payload types. The RTP packet should not have the marker bit set.

Each RTP packet containing comfort noise must contain exactly one CN payload per channel, because the payload has a variable length. If multiple audio channels are used, each channel must use the same spectral model order M.
sections.plainLanguage: A comfort noise packet looks like the start of a separate codec to the receiver, so its timestamp marks when the noise period began. It uses the assigned payload type 13 at 8 kHz, or a dynamic payload type at any other rate, and it carries exactly one noise description per channel.

sections.title: How Senders and Receivers Use It
sections.content:
An audio codec with discontinuous transmission capability generally includes voice activity detection, discontinuous transmission and comfort noise generation algorithms. The job of the voice activity detection is to discriminate between active and inactive voice segments in the input signal. During inactive voice segments the role of the comfort noise generation is to sufficiently describe the ambient noise while minimizing the transmission rate. A CN payload, or SID frame, containing a description of the noise is sent to the receiver to drive that generation.

The discontinuous transmission algorithm determines when a CN payload is transmitted. During active voice segments, packets of the voice codec are transmitted and indicated in the RTP header by the static or dynamic payload type for that codec. At the beginning of an inactive voice segment, a CN packet is transmitted in the same RTP stream and indicated by the CN payload type. The update rate is left implementation-specific: the CN packet may be sent periodically, or only when there is a significant change in the background noise characteristics. The generation algorithm at the receiver uses the information in the CN payload to update its noise model and then produce an appropriate amount of comfort noise.

When the Session Description Protocol is used to specify RTP payload information, the use of comfort noise is indicated by the inclusion of a payload type for CN on the media description line. With the RTP/AVP profile and a codec whose RTP timestamp clock rate is 8000 Hz, such as G.711, which is PCMU with static payload type 0, the static payload type 13 for CN can be used, so the media line reads m=audio 49230 RTP/AVP 0 13.

When CN is used with a codec that has a different RTP timestamp clock rate, a dynamic payload type mapping, the rtpmap attribute, is required. The memo shows CN used with the G.722.1 codec of RFC 3047:

m=audio 49230 RTP/AVP 101 102
a=rtpmap:101 G7221/16000
a=fmtp:121 bitrate=24000
a=rtpmap:102 CN/16000

Omitting a payload type for CN on the media description line implies that this comfort noise payload format will not be used, but it does not imply that silence will not be suppressed, because RTP allows discontinuous transmission on any audio payload format. The receiver can detect silence suppression on the first packet received after the silence by observing that the RTP timestamp is not contiguous with the end of the interval covered by the previous packet, even though the RTP sequence number has incremented by only one. The RTP marker bit is also normally set on such a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Three jobs sit behind the format. One decides whether the speaker is talking, one decides when to send a noise description, and one at the receiver turns the description into sound. The session description lists the noise payload type alongside the codec's own, so both ends know it is in use.

sections.title: Registered Names and Media Type
sections.content:
The memo defines a new RTP payload name and an associated MIME type, CN, with the media type audio/CN, and the payload format is also assigned payload type 13 in the RTP Payload Types table of the RTP Parameters registry kept by IANA.

The registration gives the media type name audio and the subtype name CN, with no required parameters. There is one optional parameter, rate, which specifies the RTP timestamp clock rate. That rate is usually, but not always, equal to the sampling rate, and the parameter should have the same value as the codec used together with comfort noise. The default value is 8000.

The type is only defined for transfer via RTP. The interoperability considerations are listed as none, the published specification is this document together with Appendix II of ITU-T Recommendation G.711, and the applications that use it are audio and video streaming and conferencing tools. The intended usage is COMMON, and the change controller is the IETF AVT Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is registered under the name CN, with the media type audio/CN, and it takes payload type 13 in the RTP registry. A session can say which clock rate it is using with an optional parameter, which defaults to 8000.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations discussed in the RTP specification, RFC 1889. This implies that confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption. Because the payload format is arranged end to end, encryption may be performed after encapsulation, so there is no conflict between the two operations.

As the format transports background noise, the memo says there are no significant security, confidentiality or authentication concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: The payload is protected in the same way as any other RTP traffic, by encrypting the stream. Since it carries only a description of background noise, the memo does not see a security problem with the content itself.
